inflation.note: CPI-U was 3.7% a year in Sept 2026 (BLS, energy-driven); BLS could not publish a 12-month change for Oct 2026 because Oct 2025 data were never collected. The Cleveland Fed 10-year expected inflation is 2.67% (Nov 2026 update). 3% sits between the current rate and the long-run expectation, so kept.

savings.note: FDIC national rates (16 Nov 2026): the average savings account pays 0.39%, and the national rate cap is 4.63%. Online high-yield accounts paid around 4.2–4.35% APY in Oct 2026 (The College Investor; not re-checked, the site blocks automated access). 4% assumes a high-yield account.

longTerm.note: S&P 500 with dividends returned about 10.0% a year (geometric) over 1928-2025 (Damodaran, NYU Stern); 8% is kept as a deliberately cautious long-term figure below that history.

shares.note: Matches the S&P 500 1928-2025 geometric average of about 10.0% a year with dividends (Damodaran, NYU Stern); history, never guaranteed.

cardApr.note: Federal Reserve G.19 (6 Nov 2026): commercial bank credit card rate for accounts assessed interest 22.36% in Q3 2026 (preliminary); all accounts 21.19%.

extraFields.label: Health insurance premium
extraFields.help: What you pay each month for health insurance, including the amount taken from your paycheck for an employer plan or a Marketplace plan after any tax credit.

single.note: KFF 2026: average worker contribution for single coverage $1,672 a year (about $139 a month, 18% of the $9,804 premium); the 80-200 spread around it is our estimate, KFF gives no distribution in its summary.

suburban.note: KFF 2026: average worker contribution for family coverage $7,471 a year (about $623 a month, 27% of the $28,303 premium). The spread around it, for cheaper and costlier plans, is our estimate.

youngpro.note: Between KFF 2026 single ($139 a month) and family ($623 a month) worker contributions; KFF summary has no employee-plus-spouse figure, so the range is an estimate.

localTips.title: Compare health plans at open enrollment
localTips.why: Employer and Marketplace plans change prices every year, and the default is often to roll over into the same plan.
tips: At open enrollment, compare the premium plus the deductible you realistically expect to pay, not the premium alone.
If you are both covered at work, check whether one family plan or two separate plans costs less.
If you buy on HealthCare.gov or a state Marketplace, update your income: you may qualify for a bigger tax credit.

pct.note: Assumed saving from switching plans at open enrollment; no national study of the typical saving found, estimate kept.
